title: Promises to retirees and debt, per resident
question: How much does each place owe per resident for pensions, retiree health care and borrowing?
finding: In fiscal 2024 San Francisco owed $4,668 per resident in unfunded pension promises, $4,641 in retiree-health promises and $4,915 in general-fund debt: $14,224 together. Among the 6 city-plus-county pairs the middle total was $7,698 and the highest was Oakland + Alameda County at $10,295. San Francisco’s retiree-health promise per resident is 3.0 times the pair middle; its pension promise is 1.11 times the pair middle.
how: San Francisco is a city and a county in one government. Every other city here sits inside a county that separately runs welfare, public health, jails and support for the courts for its residents, so setting San Francisco beside a city alone overstates the gap. The fairer comparison adds each city’s spending per city resident to its county’s spending per county resident. Fiscal 2024, the latest year in the State Controller’s pension and retiree-health tables. Net amounts owed (promises less money set aside) for each government’s own funds, businesses included; general-fund debt is principal owed at year end on bonds and loans listed against general funds; “all debt” adds debt of city- and county-run businesses. Each divided by the State Controller’s population estimate; pairs add the city and county figures.
limits: San Francisco employs the staff of an airport, a transit system, a water and power utility, a port and public hospitals, whose pension and retiree-health promises are in its figure; other cities with fewer businesses of their own look lighter for that reason alone, and where a separate district runs transit or water its promises appear nowhere in this table. Each pension fund chooses its own assumptions. “All debt” mostly reflects how large a place’s airport, water and power businesses are and is repaid from their charges, not from taxes. A county’s figure is spread over all its residents. The State Controller’s retiree-health table for counties repeats the pension table to the dollar for fiscal 2018 (5 of the 5 counties used here), which looks like a publishing error in the source; those cells are left out, so no pair figure is given for retiree health in that year.
